draft.title: A confidence interval is a procedure
draft.subtitle: The parameter stays fixed. The interval moves.
prerequisites: Mean and standard error of an independent sample mean.
Normal probabilities and symmetry; population standard deviation is treated as known.
outcomes: Derive a known-variance normal mean interval from a pivot.
Explain coverage without assigning a frequentist probability to a fixed parameter after observation.
Predict how sample size and confidence level affect interval width.
draft.scopeNote: Selected historical CS1 scope only. Known population standard deviation is assumed; estimating it requires methods beyond this unit.

blocks.title: A point estimate is only the beginning
blocks.text: A sample mean is useful, but another sample would produce another value. An interval adds information about the uncertainty of a procedure. It does not turn a model assumption into an observed fact.
Specify the experiment before the percentage

Assume $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ are independent normal observations with unknown mean $\mu$ and known population standard deviation $\sigma$. Then $\bar X$ is exactly normal with mean $\mu$ and standard error $\sigma/\sqrt n$. We use the data to produce a random interval whose construction is designed to contain the fixed parameter in a stated proportion of repeated samples.

A confidence level such as 95% describes the long-run coverage of that construction under the model. It is not a guarantee for the particular sample in hand. Changing the population, sampling design or model can change coverage even when a formula still displays “95%”.

The standardised quantity $Z=(\bar X-\mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)$ has a standard normal distribution under this model. Let $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ be the normal quantile leaving probability α/2 above it. Symmetry gives probability 1−α between the negative and positive quantiles. We now rearrange that probability statement to isolate μ.

blocks.title: Turn a probability statement into random endpoints

steps.title: Begin with a distribution we know
steps.text: P(−z ≤ (X̄−μ)/(σ/√n) ≤ z) = 1−α, with z = z₁₋α/₂.
steps.why: The pivot has a distribution that does not depend on the unknown mean.

steps.title: Use a positive scale
steps.text: Multiply the inequalities by σ/√n, which is positive, so their directions remain unchanged.
steps.why: The parameter domain and sample size make the scale positive.

steps.title: Isolate the parameter
steps.text: The event is equivalent to X̄−zσ/√n ≤ μ ≤ X̄+zσ/√n.
steps.why: The endpoints are random because they depend on the random sample mean.

steps.title: Observe the data
steps.text: Substitute the realised sample mean to obtain one numerical interval. The construction had coverage 1−α before seeing the sample.
steps.why: After observation the parameter and both realised endpoints are fixed in this frequentist model.

blocks.explanation: Centre the interval on the observed mean. The margin is a normal quantile multiplied by the standard error.

blocks.title: Where the 95% belongs
blocks.text: Once the numerical interval is observed, it either contains the fixed mean or it does not. The 95% refers to the performance of the interval-generating procedure over repeated samples. A probability distribution for μ after seeing data would require a different modelling framework; it does not follow from this frequentist calculation.

blocks.title: A processing-cost interval

steps.title: State the inputs
steps.text: For an independent normal sample of n = 25 costs, suppose x̄ = 104 and the known population standard deviation is 20. Use 95% confidence.
steps.why: The known population standard deviation is an assumption, not a value estimated from these 25 records.

steps.title: Compute the standard error
steps.text: 20 / √25 = 4 currency units. The 0.975 normal quantile is about 1.959964.
steps.why: Each tail has 0.025 probability under the standard normal model.

steps.title: Form the interval
steps.text: The margin is 1.959964 × 4 = 7.839856. The interval is [96.160144, 111.839856], or [96.16, 111.84] to two decimal places.
steps.why: The endpoints, not just the centre, must use consistent units and rounding.

steps.title: Interpret and check
steps.text: This is one interval generated by a procedure with 95% coverage under the stated model. Its length is 15.679712 currency units.
steps.why: The interval does not contain 95% of individual costs; it targets a population mean.

blocks.prompt: An independent normal sample has observed mean 52, known population standard deviation 12, and n = 36. Using z = 1.96, what is the lower endpoint of the 95% confidence interval?
blocks.solution: Standard error = 12/√36 = 2. Margin = 1.96×2 = 3.92. The lower endpoint is 52−3.92 = 48.08. The corresponding upper endpoint is 55.92.
hints: A lower endpoint subtracts the margin from the observed mean.

blocks.prompt: For independent normal observations with unknown mean μ and known σ>0, derive a two-sided (1−α) confidence interval for μ. Start from the standard normal pivot, show the inequality rearrangement, and identify which quantities are random before sampling.
blocks.solution: Under the model, Z=(X̄−μ)/(σ/√n) has a standard normal distribution. Put z=z₁₋α/₂. Then P(−z≤(X̄−μ)/(σ/√n)≤z)=1−α. Multiplying by the positive standard error gives the equivalent event −zσ/√n≤X̄−μ≤zσ/√n. Rearranging yields X̄−zσ/√n≤μ≤X̄+zσ/√n. Therefore the two endpoints define a random interval with coverage 1−α under the model. The endpoints depend on X̄ and are random before sampling; μ is fixed. Observing x̄ yields numerical endpoints without assigning a frequentist posterior probability to μ.

rubric.text: Specify the standard normal pivot and its model assumptions.
Allocate α/2 to each tail and state the central probability event.
Rearrange using the positive scale to obtain both correct endpoints.
Identify the random endpoints and fixed parameter before sampling.

blocks.text: Coverage and precision answer different questions

The interval length is $2z_{1-\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt n$. With the same σ and confidence level, increasing n from 25 to 100 halves the length. Increasing the confidence level instead requires a larger quantile, so it widens the interval. A narrower interval is not automatically a better statement if it achieves that narrowness by reducing coverage or ignoring important uncertainty.

For our exact model, a 99% procedure covers the mean more often in repeated samples than a 90% procedure, at the cost of wider intervals. Neither procedure makes a biased sampling design representative. If σ is unknown, replacing it with a sample standard deviation changes the pivot; the appropriate t method is outside this unit.

blocks.title: Watch the interval move, not the parameter
blocks.purpose: Separate the fixed true mean from the random intervals created by repeated normal samples.
blocks.prediction: Predict how many of 50 independently generated 95% intervals will miss the true mean. Must it be exactly two or three?
blocks.debrief: The miss count is itself random. A finite batch need not achieve exactly the nominal coverage. The fixed vertical line marks the true mean; endpoints move because samples change.
blocks.fallback: With known σ=20 and n=25, every 95% interval has theoretical length about 15.68. Repeating the procedure 50 times produces an expected 47.5 covering intervals, not a guaranteed count. The true mean does not move between repetitions.
blocks.transfer: Explain what would happen to interval length and long-run coverage if n quadrupled but the nominal confidence level stayed fixed.

blocks.prompt: After computing [96.16, 111.84], which statement matches the frequentist model?
blocks.solution: The interval is one realised output of a method with 95% repeated-sampling coverage under the model. Individual costs are not its target, and no posterior probability for the fixed mean has been specified.
options: 95% of individual processing costs lie inside these endpoints.
The fixed mean has a 95% frequentist probability of being inside these now-fixed endpoints.
The interval came from a procedure that covers the fixed mean in 95% of repeated samples under the model.
feedback: A confidence interval for a mean does not estimate an interval containing 95% of individuals.
That probability interpretation would require an additional model for the parameter; it is not this calculation.
Yes. Coverage describes the procedure before observing a particular sample.

blocks.prompt: A manager wants both shorter intervals and higher confidence. Explain why changing confidence alone cannot achieve both, and identify one model-preserving way to improve precision.
blocks.solution: Higher confidence increases the quantile and therefore widens the interval at fixed n and σ. Increasing the size of a genuinely independent representative sample reduces standard error and can offset that width increase. It does not repair selection bias.

blocks.text: If you described 95% of individual costs, return to “Where the 95% belongs”. If you assigned 95% frequentist probability to the fixed mean after observing endpoints, revisit the random-endpoint derivation and coverage lab. If higher confidence made your interval narrower, revisit “Coverage and precision answer different questions”. Explain why quadrupling n halves the width while leaving the model’s nominal coverage at 95%. Reading these endpoints is not evidence that you can reconstruct their derivation.

draft.title: A sample mean is a moving target
draft.subtitle: One population. Many possible samples. A distribution of answers.
prerequisites: Expectation, variance, independence and the shape of a normal distribution.
Summing finite sequences and interpreting a probability density.
outcomes: Separate individual variability from variability of a mean.
Derive standard error and explain what changes with sample size.
Use simulation to challenge, rather than replace, the assumptions of the central limit theorem.
draft.scopeNote: Selected historical CS1 scope only. Sample-variance distributions, t and F methods are deferred.

blocks.title: Before we calculate
blocks.text: An insurer cannot examine every administration transaction. It samples 25 records and estimates the average processing cost. If another team takes a different sample, should it obtain the same answer? The population can stay unchanged while the estimate moves.
The object that stays fixed, and the object that changes

The population is the collection or probability model about which we want to learn. A sample is the observed part we use. Statistical inference uses the sample to make a statement about a population quantity, such as its mean. A parameter belongs to the population model; a statistic is a function of the sample.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be processing costs from an independent random sample with common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Before observation, these symbols denote random variables. After sampling, their realised values are numbers. The independence assumption says that knowing one cost does not alter the distribution of another. It is a substantive assumption about selection and dependence, not a reward for collecting many records.

blocks.title: A large sample can repeat a selection error
blocks.text: If only transactions completed during quiet shifts are sampled, the result may not represent all shifts. More records from the same selected group can shrink sampling variation while leaving the selection problem. The calculations below assume the sample really comes from the stated common population.

The sample mean is $\bar X=(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n$. Once we see the sample, its value is a number. Before we see it, it is random because it is calculated from random inputs. Imagine repeating the same sampling plan many times without changing the population. The distribution of the resulting means is the sampling distribution of $\bar X$.

This is a different distribution from that of individual costs. A histogram of costs tells us how transactions differ. A histogram of means tells us how a particular estimation procedure differs between repeated samples. A histogram from one observed sample is neither a census of the population nor, by itself, a sampling distribution.

blocks.prompt: A team draws 40 new records every week and plots each week’s mean cost. If the population and sampling plan remain unchanged, which distribution is the plot trying to approximate?
blocks.solution: It approximates the sampling distribution of the mean for samples of size 40. Each plotted point is an entire sample summarised by one statistic, not one transaction.
options: The distribution of individual transaction costs
The sampling distribution of the sample mean
The probability distribution of a fixed population parameter
feedback: Each point is a mean of 40 records, not an individual record.
Yes. Repeating the sampling procedure makes the statistic vary.
The parameter is fixed in this model; our statistic is random.

blocks.text: Why averaging changes spread

Covariance describes how two random deviations move together. For finite second moments, Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−E[X])(Y−E[Y])]. A positive value means same-sign deviations contribute more on average than opposite-sign deviations; independence makes covariance zero, although zero covariance alone does not establish independence. Covariance has the product of the two variables’ units.

To see why it enters, write U=X−E[X] and V=Y−E[Y]. Then Var(X+Y)=E[(U+V)²]=E[U²]+2E[UV]+E[V²]=Var(X)+2Cov(X,Y)+Var(Y). Each pair of different variables contributes twice when the squared sum is expanded. Dividing a sum by n scales its variance by 1/n². These are the two ingredients used next.

Boundary check: suppose X₁=⋯=Xₙ=Y, all copies of the same random outcome with variance σ²>0. Then X̄=Y and Var(X̄)=σ², regardless of n. The covariance formula agrees: every distinct pair has covariance σ², giving [nσ²+n(n−1)σ²]/n²=σ². A larger row count cannot create independent information.

Linearity of expectation gives $E[\bar X]=(E[X_1]+\cdots+E[X_n])/n=\mu$. Independence is not needed for this equality when the common mean exists. For variance, multiplying a variable by $1/n$ multiplies its variance by $1/n^2$. Independence removes covariance terms, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=n\sigma^2$. Combining the two steps gives the formula below.

If the observations are positively correlated, omitted covariance terms can make the actual variance larger. It is therefore wrong to use the independent-sample formula merely because a sample contains n rows.

In general, Var(∑Xᵢ)=∑Var(Xᵢ)+2∑ᵢ<ⱼ Cov(Xᵢ,Xⱼ): the second sum includes each distinct pair once, with a factor of two. Combining this with the scale 1/n² gives the correlated-sample expression. Independence sets the pairwise covariances to zero, rather than changing linearity of expectation.

blocks.explanation: A mean stays centred on the population mean, while its standard deviation decreases with the square root of sample size. This standard deviation is called its standard error.

blocks.title: How much information does a larger sample buy?

steps.title: Define the model
steps.text: Suppose individual processing costs have mean 100 and standard deviation 20 currency units, and observations are independent.
steps.why: Individual standard deviation describes cost variability, not uncertainty in a sample mean.

steps.title: Calculate the first standard error
steps.text: For n = 25, standard error = 20 / √25 = 4 currency units.
steps.why: Taking a mean averages some individual variation away.

steps.title: Compare, rather than memorise
steps.text: For n = 100, standard error = 20 / √100 = 2. Four times as many observations halves the standard error.
steps.why: To halve 1/√n, multiply n by four. Doubling n only multiplies the standard error by 1/√2.

steps.title: Check meaning and units
steps.text: Both the mean and standard error are in currency units. The mean is still centred at 100. Larger n changes precision, not the population parameter.
steps.why: A more precise estimate is not automatically unbiased if the sample design is wrong.

blocks.prompt: Individual costs have standard deviation 18. What is the standard error of an independent sample mean based on 81 records? Give the answer in currency units.
blocks.solution: The standard error is 18/√81 = 2. The variance is 4, which has squared units and is a different answer.

blocks.text: When does the shape become normal?

For independent identically distributed observations with finite mean and finite nonzero variance, the standardised mean $\sqrt n(\bar X-\mu)/\sigma$ converges in distribution to a standard normal as n increases. There is no universal sample size that makes every tail probability accurate. Strong dependence or infinite variance can invalidate the theorem stated here.

blocks.title: Before we calculate
blocks.text: An insurer cannot examine every administration transaction. It samples 25 records and estimates the average processing cost. If another team takes a different sample, should it obtain the same answer? The population can stay unchanged while the estimate moves.
The object that stays fixed, and the object that changes

The population is the collection or probability model about which we want to learn. A sample is the observed part we use. Statistical inference uses the sample to make a statement about a population quantity, such as its mean. A parameter belongs to the population model; a statistic is a function of the sample.

Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be processing costs from an independent random sample with common mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. Before observation, these symbols denote random variables. After sampling, their realised values are numbers. The independence assumption says that knowing one cost does not alter the distribution of another. It is a substantive assumption about selection and dependence, not a reward for collecting many records.

blocks.title: A large sample can repeat a selection error
blocks.text: If only transactions completed during quiet shifts are sampled, the result may not represent all shifts. More records from the same selected group can shrink sampling variation while leaving the selection problem. The calculations below assume the sample really comes from the stated common population.

The sample mean is $\bar X=(X_1+\cdots+X_n)/n$. Once we see the sample, its value is a number. Before we see it, it is random because it is calculated from random inputs. Imagine repeating the same sampling plan many times without changing the population. The distribution of the resulting means is the sampling distribution of $\bar X$.

This is a different distribution from that of individual costs. A histogram of costs tells us how transactions differ. A histogram of means tells us how a particular estimation procedure differs between repeated samples. A histogram from one observed sample is neither a census of the population nor, by itself, a sampling distribution.

blocks.text: Why averaging changes spread

Covariance describes how two random deviations move together. For finite second moments, Cov(X,Y)=E[(X−E[X])(Y−E[Y])]. A positive value means same-sign deviations contribute more on average than opposite-sign deviations; independence makes covariance zero, although zero covariance alone does not establish independence. Covariance has the product of the two variables’ units.

To see why it enters, write U=X−E[X] and V=Y−E[Y]. Then Var(X+Y)=E[(U+V)²]=E[U²]+2E[UV]+E[V²]=Var(X)+2Cov(X,Y)+Var(Y). Each pair of different variables contributes twice when the squared sum is expanded. Dividing a sum by n scales its variance by 1/n². These are the two ingredients used next.

Boundary check: suppose X₁=⋯=Xₙ=Y, all copies of the same random outcome with variance σ²>0. Then X̄=Y and Var(X̄)=σ², regardless of n. The covariance formula agrees: every distinct pair has covariance σ², giving [nσ²+n(n−1)σ²]/n²=σ². A larger row count cannot create independent information.

Linearity of expectation gives $E[\bar X]=(E[X_1]+\cdots+E[X_n])/n=\mu$. Independence is not needed for this equality when the common mean exists. For variance, multiplying a variable by $1/n$ multiplies its variance by $1/n^2$. Independence removes covariance terms, so $\operatorname{Var}(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=n\sigma^2$. Combining the two steps gives the formula below.

If the observations are positively correlated, omitted covariance terms can make the actual variance larger. It is therefore wrong to use the independent-sample formula merely because a sample contains n rows.

In general, Var(∑Xᵢ)=∑Var(Xᵢ)+2∑ᵢ<ⱼ Cov(Xᵢ,Xⱼ): the second sum includes each distinct pair once, with a factor of two. Combining this with the scale 1/n² gives the correlated-sample expression. Independence sets the pairwise covariances to zero, rather than changing linearity of expectation.

draft.subtitle: Build a decision rule before you look at the result.
prerequisites: Independent normal sample means and their standard errors.

Calculate a normal-mean test statistic and p-value and make a conditional decision.
Distinguish Type I error, Type II error, power, and practical importance.
draft.scopeNote: Selected historical CS1 scope only. Known population standard deviation is assumed; estimating it requires methods beyond this unit.

blocks.title: A change, or ordinary sampling variation?
blocks.text: An insurer has redesigned an administrative process. The previous model used mean cost 100 per record, with known standard deviation 20. A random sample of 25 records now has mean 106. Is that enough evidence of an increase? A difference in sample means alone does not tell us how unusual the result is under an unchanged population.
Write down the question first

Use the model of independent normal costs with known σ=20. We test the simple null $H_0:\mu=100$ against the one-sided alternative $H_1:\mu>100$. The null is simple because it specifies one value for the unknown mean; the alternative is composite because it contains many possible means.

The direction should be chosen from the substantive question before examining the observed mean. If increases and decreases both matter, the alternative is $\mu\ne100$ and evidence in either tail counts. Choosing the tail after seeing which result looks more favourable changes the error properties of the procedure.

Under the null, the statistic $Z=(\bar X-100)/(20/\sqrt n)$ is standard normal. A significance level α is the probability of rejecting H₀ when this null model is true. For an upper-tail test, rejecting when Z exceeds the 1−α quantile creates an upper critical region with probability α under the null.

The significance level belongs to the rule before sampling. The observed p-value instead measures how much null-model tail probability lies at least as extreme as the observed statistic, in the pre-specified direction. It is not the probability that the null is true.

blocks.explanation: Measure the observed mean in null-model standard errors, then use the corresponding upper tail of the standard normal distribution.

blocks.title: A mean increase of six is not yet a decision

steps.title: Find the relevant scale
steps.text: For n=25 and σ=20, the standard error is 4. The observed statistic is (106−100)/4 = 1.5.
steps.why: The relevant variability is that of the mean, not the variability of an individual cost.

steps.title: Find a tail probability
steps.text: For the pre-specified upper alternative, p = 1−Φ(1.5) ≈ 0.06681.
steps.why: This is the chance, under μ=100, of a sample mean at least as large as 106.

steps.title: Apply the declared rule
steps.text: At α=0.05, the critical Z value is about 1.64485. Since 1.5 is below it, or equivalently p>0.05, do not reject the null.
steps.why: The observed result has not entered the pre-specified rejection region.

steps.title: Use careful language
steps.text: We have insufficient evidence of an increase at this level under the model. We have not proved that the mean is exactly 100.
steps.why: Not rejecting a hypothesis is different from assigning it certainty or proving equivalence.

blocks.prompt: Use the same null and σ=20, but n=100 and observed mean 106. What is the test statistic z?
blocks.solution: The standard error is 20/√100=2, so z=(106−100)/2=3. The upper-tail p-value is about 0.00135, which rejects at 5%. The observed difference stayed six, but its null-model scale changed.

blocks.text: Two ways a rule can be wrong

A Type I error rejects the null when it is true. For the exact model and continuous upper-tail rule above, its probability is α. A Type II error fails to reject when a specified alternative mean is true. Its probability depends on which alternative mean we choose. Power at that alternative is one minus its Type II error probability: the chance the rule detects the departure.

blocks.title: One fixed rule, evaluated in two worlds
Keep the rule fixed; change the probability model

steps.title: Choose the cutoff under H₀
steps.text: At α=0.05 and n=25, the upper cutoff is c=100+z₀.₉₅×4≈106.5794. This is fixed before sampling.
steps.why: The null tail above c is 0.05, which sets the false-alarm probability.

steps.title: Specify an alternative world
steps.text: If μ=108, X̄ has mean 108 and standard error 4. The rule still rejects only when X̄>c.
steps.why: Power evaluates the original decision rule; it does not redesign its cutoff around 108.

steps.title: Write the event before standardizing
steps.text: Power at 108 = P₁₀₈(X̄>c)=1−Φ((c−108)/4)≈0.63876. Type II error at 108 is the complementary probability, about 0.36124.
steps.why: Subtract the mean of the world in which the probability is evaluated. The observed sample mean is not an input to this power calculation.

blocks.text: Lowering α while keeping n fixed makes false alarms less frequent under H₀, but pushes the upper cutoff outwards and reduces power against a given increase. Increasing a valid independent sample size shrinks the standard error and can improve detection of the same departure. A p-value uses observed data and the null world; power uses a specified alternative world and the whole rejection rule. Neither is the probability that a hypothesis is true. A very small p-value does not tell us whether a difference matters commercially: estimate the change, consider its uncertainty, and relate it to costs or decisions.

In the hypothetical world μ=104, give the mean and standard error of X̄, write the power event, and complete its standardization. Use Φ(0.64485)≈0.74049 to obtain power and Type II error. Is power higher or lower than at μ=108, and why? [5 marks]

[1] Power≈1−0.74049=0.25951 and Type II error≈0.74049. [1] Power is lower than 0.63876 at 108: 104 lies farther below the same upper cutoff, with the same spread. [1] No observed sample mean or observed p-value was changed or needed.

blocks.prompt: A process has reference mean cost 50 currency units. Before data collection, the team asks specifically whether the mean has increased. blocks.title: A change, or ordinary sampling variation?
blocks.text: An insurer has redesigned an administrative process. The previous model used mean cost 100 per record, with known standard deviation 20. A random sample of 25 records now has mean 106. Is that enough evidence of an increase? A difference in sample means alone does not tell us how unusual the result is under an unchanged population.
Write down the question first

Use the model of independent normal costs with known σ=20. We test the simple null $H_0:\mu=100$ against the one-sided alternative $H_1:\mu>100$. The null is simple because it specifies one value for the unknown mean; the alternative is composite because it contains many possible means.

The direction should be chosen from the substantive question before examining the observed mean. If increases and decreases both matter, the alternative is $\mu\ne100$ and evidence in either tail counts. Choosing the tail after seeing which result looks more favourable changes the error properties of the procedure.

Under the null, the statistic $Z=(\bar X-100)/(20/\sqrt n)$ is standard normal. A significance level α is the probability of rejecting H₀ when this null model is true. For an upper-tail test, rejecting when Z exceeds the 1−α quantile creates an upper critical region with probability α under the null.

The significance level belongs to the rule before sampling. The observed p-value instead measures how much null-model tail probability lies at least as extreme as the observed statistic, in the pre-specified direction. It is not the probability that the null is true.

blocks.explanation: Measure the observed mean in null-model standard errors, then use the corresponding upper tail of the standard normal distribution.

blocks.title: A mean increase of six is not yet a decision

steps.title: Find the relevant scale
steps.text: For n=25 and σ=20, the standard error is 4. The observed statistic is (106−100)/4 = 1.5.
steps.why: The relevant variability is that of the mean, not the variability of an individual cost.

steps.title: Find a tail probability
steps.text: For the pre-specified upper alternative, p = 1−Φ(1.5) ≈ 0.06681.
steps.why: This is the chance, under μ=100, of a sample mean at least as large as 106.

steps.title: Apply the declared rule
steps.text: At α=0.05, the critical Z value is about 1.64485. Since 1.5 is below it, or equivalently p>0.05, do not reject the null.
steps.why: The observed result has not entered the pre-specified rejection region.

steps.title: Use careful language
steps.text: We have insufficient evidence of an increase at this level under the model. We have not proved that the mean is exactly 100.
steps.why: Not rejecting a hypothesis is different from assigning it certainty or proving equivalence.

blocks.prompt: Use the same null and σ=20, but n=100 and observed mean 106. What is the test statistic z?
blocks.solution: The standard error is 20/√100=2, so z=(106−100)/2=3. The upper-tail p-value is about 0.00135, which rejects at 5%. The observed difference stayed six, but its null-model scale changed.

blocks.text: Two ways a rule can be wrong

A Type I error rejects the null when it is true. For the exact model and continuous upper-tail rule above, its probability is α. A Type II error fails to reject when a specified alternative mean is true. Its probability depends on which alternative mean we choose. Power at that alternative is one minus its Type II error probability: the chance the rule detects the departure.

blocks.title: One fixed rule, evaluated in two worlds
Keep the rule fixed; change the probability model

steps.title: Choose the cutoff under H₀
steps.text: At α=0.05 and n=25, the upper cutoff is c=100+z₀.₉₅×4≈106.5794. This is fixed before sampling.
steps.why: The null tail above c is 0.05, which sets the false-alarm probability.

steps.title: Specify an alternative world
steps.text: If μ=108, X̄ has mean 108 and standard error 4. The rule still rejects only when X̄>c.
steps.why: Power evaluates the original decision rule; it does not redesign its cutoff around 108.

steps.title: Write the event before standardizing
steps.text: Power at 108 = P₁₀₈(X̄>c)=1−Φ((c−108)/4)≈0.63876. Type II error at 108 is the complementary probability, about 0.36124.
steps.why: Subtract the mean of the world in which the probability is evaluated. The observed sample mean is not an input to this power calculation.

blocks.text: Lowering α while keeping n fixed makes false alarms less frequent under H₀, but pushes the upper cutoff outwards and reduces power against a given increase. Increasing a valid independent sample size shrinks the standard error and can improve detection of the same departure. A p-value uses observed data and the null world; power uses a specified alternative world and the whole rejection rule. Neither is the probability that a hypothesis is true. A very small p-value does not tell us whether a difference matters commercially: estimate the change, consider its uncertainty, and relate it to costs or decisions.

blocks.prompt: Keep the original rule n=25, σ=20, μ₀=100, α=0.05 and c=106.5794. In the hypothetical world μ=104, give the mean and standard error of X̄, write the power event, and complete its standardization. Use Φ(0.64485)≈0.74049 to obtain power and Type II error. Is power higher or lower than at μ=108, and why? [5 marks]
blocks.solution: Under μ=104, X̄ is normal with mean 104 and standard error 4. [1] The unchanged rule gives P₁₀₄(X̄>106.5794). [1] Standardize about 104: (106.5794−104)/4≈0.64485. [1] Power≈1−0.74049=0.25951 and Type II error≈0.74049. [1] Power is lower than 0.63876 at 108: 104 lies farther below the same upper cutoff, with the same spread. [1] No observed sample mean or observed p-value was changed or needed.
